source: Uganda Clinical Guidelines / WHO Community Health Guidance

entries.text: MALARIA PREVENTION AT HOME: Malaria is spread by mosquitoes that bite mainly at night. Prevention measures: (1) Sleep under a Long-Lasting Insecticidal Net (LLIN) every night — even during dry season. (2) Ensure all family members, especially children under 5 and pregnant women, sleep under the net. (3) Tuck the net under the mattress. (4) Clear bushes around the home. (5) Drain stagnant water where mosquitoes breed. (6) Wear long sleeves in the evening. (7) If you develop fever, headache, body aches, and chills — go to the health facility for an RDT test within 24 hours. Early treatment saves lives. Do NOT buy medicine from the market without testing first.

WHEN TO SEEK CARE — GENERAL GUIDANCE: Go to the health facility if you have any of these: (1) Fever lasting more than 3 days. (2) Difficulty breathing or chest pain. (3) Severe headache with stiff neck. (4) Vomiting blood or blood in stool. (5) Sudden severe pain anywhere. (6) Injury or wound that is deep, bleeding heavily, or infected. (7) Confusion or loss of consciousness. (8) Seizures or convulsions. (9) Sudden weakness on one side of the body. (10) High fever with rash. Do not wait — delays in seeking care can lead to serious complications or death. The health facility is free for basic services.

SAFE WATER AND HYGIENE: (1) Always drink clean, safe water. Boil water for at least 1 minute or use water treatment chemicals (WaterGuard). (2) Wash hands with soap: before eating, before preparing food, after using the toilet, after changing a baby's nappy, after handling animals. (3) Use a latrine — do not defecate in the open. (4) Keep food covered and stored safely. (5) Wash fruits and vegetables before eating. (6) Keep your home and compound clean. Diarrhoea, cholera, and typhoid are caused by dirty water and poor hygiene. Hand washing with soap can reduce diarrhoea by 40%.

HIV/AIDS — WHAT EVERYONE SHOULD KNOW: (1) HIV is spread through: unprotected sex, sharing needles/sharp instruments, mother to child (during pregnancy, delivery, or breastfeeding). (2) HIV is NOT spread through: shaking hands, hugging, sharing food, mosquito bites. (3) Know your status — get tested. Testing is free and confidential at all health facilities. (4) Prevention: use condoms consistently, be faithful to one partner, avoid sharing needles. (5) If HIV positive: start ART (antiretroviral therapy) immediately. ART is FREE at government facilities. Take medicines every day at the same time. You can live a long, healthy life with HIV on treatment. (6) Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission (PMTCT): all HIV-positive pregnant women should be on ART to protect the baby.

DIABETES WARNING SIGNS AND MANAGEMENT: Diabetes is a condition where the body cannot properly control blood sugar. Warning signs: excessive thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss, blurred vision, slow-healing wounds, tingling in hands or feet, extreme fatigue. If you have these signs, go to the health facility for a blood sugar test. Management: (1) Take prescribed medicine every day as directed. (2) Eat balanced meals — reduce sugar, white bread, soda, and sweets. (3) Eat more vegetables, beans, and whole grains. (4) Exercise regularly — at least 30 minutes of walking daily. (5) Check blood sugar regularly at the clinic. (6) Care for your feet — check daily for wounds. DANGER: If you feel very dizzy, confused, or very thirsty, go to the facility IMMEDIATELY.

HYPERTENSION (HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE): Hypertension often has no symptoms but can lead to stroke, heart attack, and kidney damage. Risk factors: age, obesity, too much salt, stress, alcohol, family history. Management: (1) Take prescribed blood pressure medicine EVERY DAY — do not stop when you feel well. (2) Reduce salt in food. (3) Eat more fruits and vegetables. (4) Exercise regularly. (5) Maintain a healthy weight. (6) Limit alcohol. (7) Stop smoking. (8) Manage stress. Get your blood pressure checked at least once a year. DANGER SIGNS — go to facility immediately: severe headache, chest pain, difficulty breathing, sudden blurred vision, nosebleed that won't stop.

FIRST AID FOR COMMON INJURIES: BURNS: Cool the burn immediately with clean, cool running water for at least 20 minutes. Do NOT apply toothpaste, butter, or other home remedies. Cover with a clean, loose bandage. If the burn is large, deep, on the face/hands/genitals, or if it blisters — go to the health facility. WOUNDS: Clean with clean water and mild soap. Apply pressure with a clean cloth to stop bleeding. Cover with a clean bandage. Go to the health facility if: bleeding won't stop, the wound is deep, caused by a rusty object (needs tetanus), or shows signs of infection (redness, swelling, pus, fever). SNAKE BITE: Keep the person calm and still. Do NOT cut, suck, or apply tourniquet. Go to the health facility IMMEDIATELY for antivenom.

TUBERCULOSIS (TB): TB is spread through the air when a person with TB coughs, sneezes, or spits. Symptoms: persistent cough for more than 2 weeks, coughing blood, fever (especially at night), weight loss, night sweats, chest pain. If you have a cough lasting more than 2 weeks, go to the health facility for a TB test (free). Treatment: TB is curable! Take the full 6-month course of medicine as prescribed. Do NOT stop treatment when you feel better — incomplete treatment leads to drug-resistant TB. Prevention: cover mouth when coughing, ensure good ventilation in homes, BCG vaccination for newborns. People living with HIV are at higher risk for TB and should be screened regularly.

SKIN RASHES — COMMON TYPES AND MANAGEMENT: Skin problems are among the most common reasons for health visits in Uganda. SCABIES: Caused by tiny mites that burrow into the skin. Signs: intense itching (worse at night), small red bumps and lines between fingers, on wrists, elbows, armpits, waist, genitals. Often affects the whole family. TREATMENT: Apply Benzyl Benzoate 25% lotion (BBL) to the ENTIRE body from neck down (not the face, except in infants). Leave on for 24 hours, then wash off. Repeat after 7 days. Treat ALL family members at the same time. Wash all bedding and clothes in hot water. FUNGAL INFECTIONS (Ringworm/Tinea): Round, red, scaly patches with a clear center. Common on scalp in children (hair loss patch), body, feet (athlete's foot). TREATMENT: Apply antifungal cream (Clotrimazole or Whitfield's ointment) twice daily for 2-4 weeks. Keep skin clean and dry. For scalp ringworm — refer for oral antifungal. ALLERGIC RASH: Red, itchy rash that may have raised bumps (hives/urticaria). Common triggers: new soap, food, insect bites, medications. TREATMENT: Antihistamine (Chlorpheniramine or Cetirizine), avoid the trigger. WHEN TO REFER: Rash with fever and joint pain, rash that blisters or bleeds, rash that does not improve after 2 weeks of treatment, rash in an HIV-positive patient, widespread skin peeling, rash with eye involvement.

EYE INFECTIONS — CONJUNCTIVITIS AND RED EYE: Red eye is very common in Uganda, especially in children. Most cases are conjunctivitis (infection or irritation of the outer eye lining). TYPES: BACTERIAL CONJUNCTIVITIS: Red eye with yellow/green pus discharge, eyelids may stick together in the morning, usually starts in one eye then spreads to the other. VIRAL CONJUNCTIVITIS: Red, watery eyes, light sensitivity, often with cold symptoms. Usually clears in 7-10 days without treatment. ALLERGIC CONJUNCTIVITIS: Itchy, watery, both eyes, seasonal. NEWBORN CONJUNCTIVITIS (Ophthalmia neonatorum): Pus from eyes within first 28 days — this is an EMERGENCY, can cause blindness. REFER IMMEDIATELY. MANAGEMENT: (1) CLEANING: Wash hands before and after touching the eyes. Clean discharge from eyes with clean cotton wool soaked in clean water — wipe from inner corner outward. Use a new piece for each eye. (2) ANTIBIOTIC DROPS: Tetracycline eye ointment 1% — apply inside the lower eyelid 3 times daily for 7 days. Or Chloramphenicol eye drops 0.5% — 1 drop 4 times daily for 7 days. (3) PREVENTION: Do not share face towels, wash hands frequently, avoid touching eyes. WHEN TO REFER: Eye pain (not just irritation), vision changes or blurred vision, sensitivity to light, injury to the eye, pus in a newborn, no improvement after 5 days of antibiotic treatment, one-sided red eye with severe pain (possible glaucoma or iritis — urgent).

EAR PAIN AND DISCHARGE — OTITIS MEDIA: Ear infections (otitis media) are very common in children under 5 in Uganda. SIGNS: Ear pain (young children may pull or rub the ear, cry, be irritable), fever, discharge (pus) from the ear, not feeding well, difficulty sleeping, hearing difficulty. TYPES: ACUTE OTITIS MEDIA: Ear pain with fever, no discharge yet. The ear drum may be bulging. CHRONIC SUPPURATIVE OTITIS MEDIA: Ear discharge lasting more than 2 weeks. This can cause permanent hearing damage. MANAGEMENT AT COMMUNITY LEVEL: (1) Pain relief: Paracetamol by weight — 15 mg/kg every 6 hours as needed. (2) DRY EAR: Keep the ear dry — do NOT put water, oil, or any liquid into the ear. Do NOT use cotton buds (push infection deeper). (3) WICKING: If there is discharge, gently clean the outer ear with a dry wick (rolled clean tissue paper) — insert gently, let it absorb the discharge, replace until dry. Do this 3 times daily. (4) ANTIBIOTIC EAR DROPS: If available, Ciprofloxacin ear drops for chronic discharge (only on prescription). (5) Oral antibiotics: Amoxicillin 25-50 mg/kg/day in 3 doses for 5 days (for acute otitis media with fever). WHEN TO REFER: Ear pain with swelling behind the ear (possible mastoiditis — urgent), ear discharge for more than 2 weeks despite treatment, hearing loss, dizziness or balance problems, ear discharge after head injury (possible skull fracture — urgent), recurrent ear infections (more than 3 in 6 months).

entries.text: URINARY SYMPTOMS — UTI MANAGEMENT: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are common, especially in women and girls. They can become serious if not treated promptly. SYMPTOMS: Pain or burning during urination (dysuria), needing to urinate frequently (frequency), urgent need to urinate, lower abdominal or pelvic pain, cloudy or smelly urine, blood in urine, fever with chills (may indicate kidney infection). IN CHILDREN: Fever without obvious source, crying when urinating, foul-smelling urine, poor feeding, irritability. IN PREGNANT WOMEN: UTIs are more common and more dangerous — can cause preterm labour. All pregnant women should be screened at first ANC visit. MANAGEMENT: (1) Drink plenty of clean water (at least 8 cups per day) to flush out bacteria. (2) Do not hold urine — urinate when you feel the need. (3) Wipe from front to back after using the toilet (women). (4) ANTIBIOTICS — refer for urine test and treatment. Common treatment: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days, or Amoxicillin-Clavulanate. Pregnant women: Nitrofurantoin or Amoxicillin (safe in pregnancy — avoid in third trimester for Nitrofurantoin). (5) Complete the full course of antibiotics even if symptoms improve. WHEN TO REFER: Fever with back pain (flank pain) — possible kidney infection (pyelonephritis), blood in urine, symptoms not improving after 3 days of antibiotics, UTI in a pregnant woman (always refer), recurrent UTIs (more than 3 per year), UTI in a male (uncommon — needs investigation), UTI in a child (needs investigation for abnormality). PREVENTION: Drink adequate water, urinate after sexual intercourse, avoid douching, good perineal hygiene, wear cotton underwear.
